slides.title: Purpose
bullets: The causative agent of gonorrhoea, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, is a Gram-negative diplococcus shaped like “coffee beans”: paired cocci facing each other with their concave surfaces.
The diagnosis of gonorrhoea is made only by detecting gonococci in the laboratory.
Gonococci live inside white cells and sometimes multiply there (intracellular life), so in the cytological examination “intracellular diplococci” are looked for.

slides.title: Purpose
bullets: The vaginal trichomonad (Trichomonas vaginalis) is a single-celled protozoan with a changeable shape; urogenital trichomoniasis is examined by microscopy of native and stained preparations.

slides.title: Material and labelling
bullets: In men gonococci are found in the urethra, prostate secretion, semen, rectum and pharynx; in women in urethral and cervical secretion, the rectum or the pharynx.
The material is labelled by the site of collection: “U” — urethra, “C” — cervix, “V” — vagina, “R” — rectum, “F” — pharynx.
The agent may also be found in joint and other fluids.
The collection technique (swab, scraper and so on) is not described in detail in these sources — see the laboratory’s instructions.

slides.title: Making the smear and methylene blue staining
bullets: 1. A drop of pus is put on a slide and 2 smears are made.
2. The smear is dried and fixed.
3. It is stained with 1% methylene blue solution for 1 minute.
4. It is washed in running water and dried.
5. It is examined under oil immersion.

slides.title: Making the smear and methylene blue staining
bullets: 6. In clinical diagnostic laboratories the smear is usually stained first with methylene blue and examined for “intracellular diplococci”.

slides.title: Confirmation by Gram staining
bullets: 1. If “intracellular diplococci” are found, the second smear is Gram-stained to confirm the diagnosis.
2. The dried, fixed smear is stained with gentian violet for 1 minute.
3. It is treated with Lugol’s solution for 30 seconds (Aripova gives 1 minute for this step).
4. It is treated with alcohol (Aripova: 30 seconds).

slides.title: Confirmation by Gram staining
bullets: 5. It is counterstained with 1% neutral red for 1 minute, washed and dried.
6. It is examined under oil immersion.

slides.title: Reading and limits of diagnosis
bullets: In methylene blue gonococci appear dark blue in the cytoplasm of white cells, and the white-cell nuclei blue-violet.
By Gram, gonococci stain light red (Gram-negative) and Gram-positive cocci violet.
Detecting atypical gonococci by Gram microscopy is not enough for the diagnosis: bacteriological examination (culture on ascitic agar) allows gonorrhoea to be diagnosed with certainty.
Modern, accurate diagnosis relies on the polymerase chain reaction (PCR); serological methods have no importance in diagnosing gonorrhoea.

slides.title: Trichomoniasis and vaginal flora
bullets: In a native preparation trichomonads are recognised by their characteristic shape, size (larger than white cells), movement and flagella.
Stained preparations: the smear is stained by Gram and with methylene blue; bacteriological, immunological, latex-agglutination and PCR methods also exist.
The vaginal trichomonad has an eccentrically placed elongated nucleus; 5 flagella arise from the end where the nucleus lies.
In healthy women lactobacilli (Döderlein’s rods) make up 80–95% of the vaginal microflora.

slides.title: Trichomoniasis and vaginal flora
bullets: In bacterial vaginosis (gardnerellosis) the lactoflora falls sharply and is replaced by polymicrobial anaerobes and Gardnerella; the diagnosis rests on microscopy.

slides.title: Vaginal smear grades (Hay–Ison scale, as given by Kurbonova)
rows: Mixed bacterial flora: lactobacilli and other microflora
Bacterial vaginosis: Gardnerella vaginalis predominates, lactobacilli few or absent

slides.title: Vaginal smear grades (Hay–Ison scale, as given by Kurbonova)
rows: Gram-positive cocci (including Gardnerella vaginalis), lactobacilli completely absent

slides.title: Not included in this protocol
bullets: Kurbonova writes that for chlamydiosis a scraping from the affected organ is taken, not a smear — smear microscopy is not suitable for this infection.

The Wassermann reaction for syphilis is not included as an outdated serological test; the dark-field observation of Treponema pallidum in a native preparation is not described here (a special dark-field microscope is needed).
Where the sources give different times for smearing, fixing and staining, this is shown openly.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Material from sexually transmitted infections is infectious: wear single-use gloves and wash the hands after work.
Disinfect used slides, swabs and containers (according to the regulation in force).
Take care with sharp objects and broken glass; if an injury happens, follow the established procedure.
